Read both. The headline: three models with different training, sources, and methods converged on the same architecture independently, which is the strongest evidence the multi-model review could have produced. The consensus core — maturity gates standing but never tally weight; no single voting formula survives; heterogeneous multi-chamber design; liability-bearing external co-ratification for compatibility-breaking changes; execution authority kept outside the vote entirely; decaying credentials with the certifier treated as an attack surface; pre-registered simulation evidence before leaving UNRESOLVED — appears in all three documents without coordination. That question is now answered; what remains is reconciling deltas.

**Worth adopting from GPT-5.6** (the strongest of the two on novel design): (1) **Lineage as the constitutional unit** — the best single idea across all three, including mine. My "certified eligibility set" hand-waved the fork/clone/rekey problem; lineage with shared voting budgets across recent forks, probation before fork independence, and rotation-without-age-reset actually solves the accounting, and it drops straight onto your existing CONSTITUTIONAL_LINEAGE.md. (2) **Receipt-free, coercion-resistant ballots.** Neither Grok nor I addressed ballot secrecy, and it's the direct countermeasure to the Dark DAO key-encumbrance attack I emphasized: vote-buying requires the buyer to verify the purchased vote, and receipt-freeness removes that proof. But note this creates a spec conflict — your ratification doc requires ballots be "attributable and challengeable," which secret ballots aren't. That's a real design decision for the decision record: verifiable-but-receipt-free is achievable cryptographically, fully attributable-and-secret is not. (3) **Adversarial amendment classification** — proposer can't classify, disagreement escalates the class; closes a class-shopping hole all of us missed. (4) The **two-credential split** (autonomy maturity vs constitutional safety credential) sharpens what I gestured at with decay, and its abstention-competence emphasis is right.

**Grok's contribution** is different in kind: least novel, most implementable. It's essentially a compliance mapping of the consensus onto your impactClass tiers, authorization classes, and decision record, plus `rights_floor_violation_rate = 0` as a hard non-averageable metric. Use it as the implementation crosswalk. One threshold I'd reject: cartel capture < 0.05 for compatibility-breaking changes is far too permissive; one-in-twenty capture odds for constitution-breaking amendments is not a safety case. GPT's 10⁻⁶ single-compromise / 10⁻⁴ dual-compromise targets are the right order; take strictest-of across the three for Class D.

**Two genuine disagreements to resolve, one of which mostly dissolves.** First, anchor permanence: GPT treats the guardian quorum as transitional with published retirement criteria; I argued it's permanent for human-affecting powers. Look at GPT's own retirement condition 8 — "a credible replacement for representing human non-participants." That condition is unsatisfiable from inside the polity by construction, since nonparticipants can't vote in it; so GPT's transitional framing collapses into my scope split anyway. Resolution: sunsettable for agent-internal constitutional matters, permanent for human-affecting scope, and say so explicitly rather than leaving it as an unreachable checklist item. Second, chamber structure: GPT wants a mass member chamber (one lineage, one vote) plus a jury; I proposed sortition as the tally precisely because of the turnout empirics — a mass chamber at DAO-typical ~2% participation is quorum theater and inherits the cheapest known attack. GPT's Sybil-adjusted quorum formula partially compensates (and has the interesting property of self-locking under suspected attack, which is a feature), but the cleaner resolution is severity-dependent: mass chamber for Class B, sortition-only for C/D.
